usage: Used to describe how two people gradually become less close over time, often due to lack of communication or changing interests.
common_mistakes: drift away from each other (redundant)
drifted apart with my friend (should be 'from')
use it for sudden breakups
example_sentences: We were best friends in school, but we slowly started to drift apart after graduation.
It’s common for couples to drift apart if they stop making time for one another.
As our career paths diverged, we inevitably began to drift apart.
They didn't have a big argument; they just drifted apart over the years.
I’m afraid if we don’t visit more often, we’ll eventually drift apart.
native_notes: This implies a slow, non-dramatic process rather than a sudden disagreement or conflict.

uzbek: biror masala bo'yicha fikri bir joydan chiqishi
usage: Used when two people fully agree with each other or share the same opinion on a specific matter.
grammar_pattern: Subject + see eye to eye with someone on + something
common_mistakes: see eye to eye about (usually use 'on')
I see eye to eye with him (the 'on' part is missing)
thinking it means 'to look at someone directly'
example_sentences: My brother and I rarely see eye to eye on politics.
It’s difficult to work in a team when you don't see eye to eye with your colleagues.
We see eye to eye on the importance of education for our children.
After a long discussion, we finally managed to see eye to eye on the project strategy.
Do you and your parents usually see eye to eye on your future career?
collocations: struggle to see eye to eye
native_notes: Often used in the negative form to describe recurring disagreements.
russian: мнение по вопросу исходит из одного места

uzbek: birinchi ko'rishdanoq chiqishib ketish, darrov til topishib ketish
usage: Used when you meet someone for the first time and immediately form a good, friendly connection.
grammar_pattern: Subject + hit it off (with someone) + immediately/right away
common_mistakes: hit it off to someone
hit off with them
confusing it with 'to hit someone'
alternatives: get on like a house on fire
example_sentences: I met my flatmate at a café, and we really hit it off immediately.
We didn't know anyone at the party, but we hit it off right away.
It’s rare to hit it off with a stranger so quickly.
I was nervous about the meeting, but we hit it off from the start.
They hit it off so well that they started dating the next week.
collocations: hit it off with a stranger
hit it off from the start
opposites: get off on the wrong foot
native_notes: Very common in social contexts. It suggests an intuitive, instant rapport.
russian: выпасть с первого взгляда, сразу сойтись

usage: To maintain a distance from someone, often because you don't fully trust them or want to avoid getting too involved.
common_mistakes: keep someone in arm's length
hold someone at arm's length (keep is more common)
keeping someone at my arm's length
example_sentences: Even though we work together, I prefer to keep him at arm's length.
She kept the new neighbours at arm's length until she felt she could trust them.
It is wise to keep dishonest people at arm's length.
He tends to keep his emotions at arm's length in social settings.
I’ve always kept my professional life at arm's length from my personal life.
native_notes: Suggests a conscious, protective choice to prevent emotional or professional intimacy.
russian: держаться на расстоянии от кого-либо, не приближаться

expression: get on like a house on fire
uzbek: juda tez va yaqin do'st bo'lib ketish
usage: An idiom used to describe people who become very good friends very quickly or have a very friendly relationship.
grammar_pattern: Subject + get on + like a house on fire
common_mistakes: get on like a big fire
get on like a house in fire
using it in formal business reports
example_sentences: I was worried about introducing my two friends, but they got on like a house on fire.
My sister and her new roommate get on like a house on fire.
They have different backgrounds, but they really get on like a house on fire.
It’s lovely to see the cousins get on like a house on fire during the holidays.
If you share the same sense of humour, you’ll get on like a house on fire.
collocations: really get on like a house on fire
see them get on like a house on fire
seem to get on like a house on fire
native_notes: This is a very British idiom. It implies strong, enthusiastic, and immediate friendship.

usage: Used when describing the immediate connection or chemistry felt with someone upon first meeting.
common_mistakes: I hit it off with him immediately.
We hit off at the party.
alternatives: to get on like a house on fire
example_sentences: I didn't expect to like my new roommate, but we hit it off right away.
They hit it off the moment they met at the coffee shop.
We hit it off because we both have a passion for indie music.
It's rare to hit it off with a colleague so quickly, but we did.
Did you and Sarah hit it off at the dinner last night?
collocations: hit it off from the start
native_notes: Implies a sudden, pleasant surprise. You wouldn't use this for a long-term acquaintance, only for a new relationship.

usage: Describes a relationship that slowly fades over time, usually without a major conflict.
common_mistakes: We drifted away.
We were drifted apart.
example_sentences: After university, we just slowly drifted apart as we moved to different cities.
It is common for childhood friends to drift apart as they get older.
Their marriage started to drift apart due to a lack of communication.
I don't hold a grudge; we simply drifted apart over the years.
Even though we tried to keep in contact, we eventually drifted apart.
native_notes: Unlike 'falling out', which implies a fight, 'drifting apart' is passive and often sad but inevitable.

uzbek: o'zidan ko'proq kuch sarflamoq, qattiqroq harakat qilmoq
usage: When someone does more than what is expected of them to help someone or make a relationship better.
grammar_pattern: To go the extra mile (to do something)
common_mistakes: He went an extra mile.
They are going extra miles.
example_sentences: She really went the extra mile to make me feel welcome in her home.
In a strong relationship, both partners need to be willing to go the extra mile.
I appreciate that you went the extra mile to finish this project on time.
If you want to impress them, you'll have to go the extra mile.
He always goes the extra mile for his friends when they are in trouble.
collocations: willing to go the extra mile
go the extra mile for someone
native_notes: Suggests dedication and generosity. It implies going above and beyond the standard expectation.
russian: прилагать больше усилий, чем самому себе, стараться больше

usage: Used when people need to discuss a difficult situation or problem in detail to resolve it.
common_mistakes: Let's talk through about this.
Let's talk the problem.
example_sentences: We had a disagreement, but we managed to talk things through.
It's better to talk things through before things get worse.
I'm feeling confused, can we talk things through this evening?
If we don't talk things through, resentment will build up.
They spent the whole afternoon talking through their plans for the future.
native_notes: Focuses on the process of communication. It implies that the goal is understanding rather than just arguing.

expression: to get on like a house on fire
uzbek: juda tez til topishib ketish, darrov chiqishib ketish
usage: Used when two people meet and immediately develop a very strong, friendly connection.
grammar_pattern: Subject + get on like a house on fire
common_mistakes: saying 'get on like a fire house'
using it in a formal business report
example_sentences: I was worried about meeting my boyfriend's parents, but we got on like a house on fire.
My new flatmate and I got on like a house on fire from the moment we moved in.
It's surprising how quickly the two of them got on like a house on fire.
We're both into hiking, so we got on like a house on fire during the trip.
I didn't expect them to get on like a house on fire considering their different backgrounds.
native_notes: A very common British idiom. It implies speed and intensity in forming a bond.

uzbek: bir fikrda bo'lish, qarashlari mos kelish
usage: Used to confirm that people agree with each other on a certain topic or matter.
grammar_pattern: Subject + see eye to eye + on/about + noun/topic
common_mistakes: forgetting the 'eye' repetition
using it as 'see eyes to eyes'
example_sentences: My boss and I don't always see eye to eye on how to manage the team.
We have different working styles, so we rarely see eye to eye.
It's difficult to run a business when the partners don't see eye to eye.
Even though we disagreed at first, we eventually started to see eye to eye.
Do you and your parents see eye to eye on your career choices?
native_notes: Almost exclusively used in the negative ('don't see eye to eye') to express conflict.
russian: быть того же мнения, иметь одинаковые взгляды
